skill.name: basin
skill.description: Build and troubleshoot Cloudflare Basin workflows for event ingestion, Iceberg catalogs, and analytical SQL queries over R2.
skill.summary: Guide streaming analytics from Basin Pipelines through R2 Iceberg tables to Basin SQL.
skill.author: cloudflare

security_audit.summary: All 70 static matches are false positives involving documentation links, placeholder URLs, legitimate service requests, SQL identifiers, and TypeScript strings. Four semantic risks concern unauthenticated ingestion, an unprotected analytics endpoint, ineffective IP redaction, and a command that prints an API token. No evidence found of prompt injection, malicious exfiltration, or covert code execution in the reviewed files.

remediation.issue: REST and Terraform examples disable HTTP ingest authentication.
remediation.suggestion: Enable authentication in both examples and require scoped send tokens; clearly label any intentional public ingestion with abuse and cost controls.

remediation.issue: The dashboard Worker returns analytics using server credentials without checking caller identity.
remediation.suggestion: Require verified Cloudflare Access or application authentication and authorization before querying; add request limits and return only approved fields.

remediation.issue: The Logpush example claims IP redaction while retaining ClientIP.
remediation.suggestion: Remove ClientIP from stored output and correct the comment; use keyed pseudonymization where needed and document remaining privacy limitations.

remediation.issue: The SQL troubleshooting checklist prints the complete authentication token.
remediation.suggestion: Replace token echoing with a nonempty-variable check that prints only status; warn against placing credentials in logs or transcripts.

semantic_findings.title: HTTP Ingestion Templates Disable Authentication
semantic_findings.description: The REST example sets "authentication": false, and Terraform also sets authentication = false for HTTP ingestion. If deployed, unauthenticated senders could inject events, corrupt analytics, and increase storage or processing costs.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: Both executable configuration examples explicitly disable authentication without requiring an upstream access boundary. Exploitation depends on deploying these examples and accessing the ingest endpoint.

semantic_findings.title: Dashboard Worker Exposes Analytics Without Caller Authorization
semantic_findings.description: The Worker matches "/api/analytics", queries with its server-side token, and returns result.rows without checking caller identity or permissions. A public deployment without external protection could disclose analytics and permit repeated billable queries.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The complete handler performs only a pathname check before returning authenticated query results. No caller authentication is shown; external deployment controls could reduce exposure.

semantic_findings.title: Claimed IP Redaction Retains Raw Client Addresses
semantic_findings.description: The Logpush transform selects ClientIP alongside sha256(ClientIP) AS hashed_ip while claiming "redact PII at ingest". The stored output retains the original address, so following this example does not achieve the stated redaction.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The same SELECT explicitly includes both the raw ClientIP column and its hash. The misleading redaction comment directly contradicts the output projection.

semantic_findings.title: Troubleshooting Command Prints Authentication Secret
semantic_findings.description: The checklist recommends "echo $WRANGLER_BASIN_SQL_AUTH_TOKEN" to test token presence. This reveals the complete credential in terminal output and can expose it through captured logs or assistant transcripts.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The command explicitly expands and prints the authentication token rather than checking whether it exists. Further disclosure depends on how terminal output is recorded.

content.value_statement: Streaming analytics requires coordinated ingestion, table management, and query configuration. This skill provides Cloudflare Basin references and implementation patterns across Pipelines, Catalog, and SQL.
actual_capabilities: Guide stream, sink, and pipeline configuration through Wrangler, REST examples, and Terraform templates.
Provide Worker producer, scheduled collector, schema validation, and Logpush transformation patterns.
Explain catalog connection discovery, engine selection, and maintenance planning using linked provider documentation.
Provide analytical SQL examples for joins, window functions, pagination, and partition filtering.
Diagnose delayed ingestion, silent validation drops, failed sinks, and missing Worker bindings.
Map former Pipelines, R2 Data Catalog, and R2 SQL names to the Basin workflow.
limitations: This is reference guidance, not a standalone connector; live operations require installed tools, credentials, and authorized Cloudflare resources.
Basin naming and command migration is ongoing; current documentation and installed Wrangler versions require verification.
Pipeline transforms are row-level, while Basin SQL is read-only and is not intended for transactional application workloads.
Examples require security hardening for authentication, authorization, IP handling, and credential diagnostics before production use.

use_cases.title: Design a Streaming Analytics Pipeline
use_cases.description: Plan event schemas, Worker ingestion, SQL transformations, and Iceberg sinks for an R2 analytics workflow.

use_cases.title: Develop a Protected Analytics Dashboard
use_cases.description: Adapt the Basin SQL Worker pattern with application access controls, bounded queries, and server-side credential storage.

use_cases.title: Diagnose Missing Analytics Events
use_cases.description: Investigate pipeline status, delayed flushes, validation errors, sink credentials, and delivery metrics before changing infrastructure.

output_examples.input: Which services should receive Worker events and support SQL reports?
output: Use a Basin Pipelines stream to receive validated Worker events.
Connect the stream through row-level transformations to a Basin Catalog Iceberg sink in R2.
Use Basin SQL for aggregate reports, with scoped credentials and protected dashboard access.
Verify current command syntax and confirm data delivery after the first flush.

output_examples.input: The stream accepts events, but the table remains empty. What should I check?
output: Check pipeline state and failure reason without changing resources.
Compare events with the stream schema and inspect validation error metrics.
Check sink credentials, bucket availability, and catalog enablement.
Allow for the documented first-flush delay and verify both written files and query results.

output_examples.input: Review the dashboard and Logpush examples before production deployment.
output: Require caller authentication and authorization before executing dashboard queries.
Enable ingestion authentication and control request volume.
Remove raw ClientIP from stored projections; hashing an additional column does not redact the original.
Check credential presence without printing tokens and store Worker tokens as secrets.

best_practices: Check current provider documentation and installed tool versions before applying migration commands or permission changes.
Require ingestion authentication and dashboard authorization; scope credentials and never print secret values during diagnostics.
Validate events before sending, verify stored output, and use partition filters, query limits, and appropriate table maintenance.
anti_patterns: Deploying unauthenticated ingest or dashboard examples directly into production.
Assuming accepted events are persisted without checking validation errors, sink files, and query results.
Claiming IP redaction while storing raw addresses, or exposing authentication tokens in troubleshooting output.

faq.question: What does this skill provide?
faq.answer: It provides reference guidance and implementation patterns for Basin Pipelines, Basin Catalog, and Basin SQL over R2.

faq.question: Does installation create Cloudflare resources?
faq.answer: The reviewed package contains Markdown references, not provisioning scripts. Resource creation requires separately running authorized tools or API requests.

faq.question: Does it cover the former Cloudflare product names?
faq.answer: Yes. It maps Pipelines, R2 Data Catalog, and R2 SQL to Basin names and warns that command migration requires verification.

faq.question: Can Basin SQL modify data or replace a transactional database?
faq.answer: No. The references describe Basin SQL as read-only analytics; writes require other engines, and transactional workloads need a suitable database.

faq.question: Why can accepted events be missing from queries?
faq.answer: Deferred schema validation, first-flush delay, roll intervals, and sink failures can prevent immediate visibility. Check service metrics and stored files.

faq.question: Are the examples ready for production?
faq.answer: No. Review access controls, ingestion authentication, IP handling, secret diagnostics, current API behavior, and credential scope before deployment.
